Complex Vector Spaces, Hermitian and Unitary Matrices

Purdue University

Complex vectors and inner products¶

We used complex numbers to keep track of amplitude and phase. If several amplitudes belong to the same system, we can collect them into a vector. The entries can now be complex, but matrix multiplication and changes of basis work as before.

For example,

v=(1i).\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}1\\i\end{pmatrix}.v=(1i​).
(1)

There is one operation we need to reconsider: the dot product. If we use the real-vector formula, this nonzero vector would have

vTv=1+i2=0.\mathbf v^T\mathbf v=1+i^2=0.vTv=1+i2=0.
(2)

That cannot serve as its squared length. Instead, conjugate the entries of the first vector:

v†v=(1−i)(1i)=1+(−i)i=2.\mathbf v^\dagger\mathbf v =\begin{pmatrix}1&-i\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}1\\i\end{pmatrix} =1+(-i)i=2.v†v=(1​−i​)(1i​)=1+(−i)i=2.
(3)

The dagger denotes the conjugate transpose:

A†=(A∗)T,(A†)nm=Amn∗.\mathbf A^\dagger=(\mathbf A^*)^T,\qquad (A^\dagger)_{nm}=A_{mn}^*.A†=(A∗)T,(A†)nm​=Amn∗​.
(4)

A star means complex conjugation without transposing. For a column vector, the dagger produces a row vector:

v†=(v1∗,…,vn∗).\mathbf v^\dagger=(v_1^*,\ldots,v_n^*).v†=(v1∗​,…,vn∗​).
(5)

For two complex column vectors, the same row-times-column calculation gives

u†v=∑mum∗vm,∥v∥2=v†v=∑m∣vm∣2.\mathbf u^\dagger\mathbf v=\sum_m u_m^*v_m, \qquad \|\mathbf v\|^2=\mathbf v^\dagger\mathbf v=\sum_m|v_m|^2.u†v=m∑​um∗​vm​,∥v∥2=v†v=m∑​∣vm​∣2.
(6)

The product can be complex, but the squared length is real and nonnegative. Multiplying a vector by a phase leaves its length unchanged.

We conjugate the first vector throughout; some mathematics texts conjugate the second instead, so check the convention when comparing formulas. We will introduce the bra-ket notation used in physics below.

Conjugate transpose of a product¶

Just as transposing reverses the order of a product, taking the conjugate transpose gives

(AB)†=B†A†,(Av)†=v†A†.(\mathbf A\mathbf B)^\dagger=\mathbf B^\dagger\mathbf A^\dagger, \qquad (\mathbf A\mathbf v)^\dagger=\mathbf v^\dagger\mathbf A^\dagger.(AB)†=B†A†,(Av)†=v†A†.
(7)
Proof 1

Consider one matrix element of the conjugate transpose:

[(AB)†]nm=[(AB)mn]∗=(∑kAmkBkn)∗=∑kBkn∗Amk∗=∑k(B†)nk(A†)km=(B†A†)nm.\begin{aligned} \big[(\mathbf A\mathbf B)^\dagger\big]_{nm} &=\big[(\mathbf A\mathbf B)_{mn}\big]^*\\ &=\left(\sum_k A_{mk}B_{kn}\right)^*\\ &=\sum_k B_{kn}^*A_{mk}^*\\ &=\sum_k (B^\dagger)_{nk}(A^\dagger)_{km}\\ &=(\mathbf B^\dagger\mathbf A^\dagger)_{nm}. \end{aligned}[(AB)†]nm​​=[(AB)mn​]∗=(k∑​Amk​Bkn​)∗=k∑​Bkn∗​Amk∗​=k∑​(B†)nk​(A†)km​=(B†A†)nm​.​
(8)

Because every matrix element agrees, (AB)†=B†A†(\mathbf A\mathbf B)^\dagger=\mathbf B^\dagger\mathbf A^\dagger(AB)†=B†A†. Taking B\mathbf BB to be the column vector v\mathbf vv gives (Av)†=v†A†(\mathbf A\mathbf v)^\dagger=\mathbf v^\dagger\mathbf A^\dagger(Av)†=v†A†.

The order reverses because transposing a product reverses its order. We will use this identity repeatedly when moving a matrix from one side of an inner product to the other.

Bra-ket notation¶

In quantum mechanics and much of physics, a column vector is called a ket and is written

∣v⟩⟷v=(v1v2⋮vn).|v\rangle \quad\longleftrightarrow\quad \mathbf v= \begin{pmatrix}v_1\\v_2\\\vdots\\v_n\end{pmatrix}.∣v⟩⟷v=⎝⎛​v1​v2​⋮vn​​⎠⎞​.
(9)

Taking the conjugate transpose produces a row vector called a bra:

⟨v∣=(∣v⟩)†⟷v†=(v1∗v2∗⋯vn∗).\langle v| =(|v\rangle)^\dagger \quad\longleftrightarrow\quad \mathbf v^\dagger =\begin{pmatrix}v_1^*&v_2^*&\cdots&v_n^*\end{pmatrix}.⟨v∣=(∣v⟩)†⟷v†=(v1∗​​v2∗​​⋯​vn∗​​).
(10)

The bra is not merely the transpose of the ket. Its entries are also complex conjugated. For example,

∣v⟩=(1i),⟨v∣=(1−i).|v\rangle=\begin{pmatrix}1\\i\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \langle v|=\begin{pmatrix}1&-i\end{pmatrix}.∣v⟩=(1i​),⟨v∣=(1​−i​).
(11)

Placing a bra and ket together gives their inner product:

⟨u∣v⟩=u†v,⟨v∣v⟩=∥v∥2.\boxed{\langle u|v\rangle=\mathbf u^\dagger\mathbf v}, \qquad \langle v|v\rangle=\|\mathbf v\|^2.⟨u∣v⟩=u†v​,⟨v∣v⟩=∥v∥2.
(12)

The result is a scalar. Reversing the order conjugates that scalar:

⟨v∣u⟩=⟨u∣v⟩∗.\langle v|u\rangle=\langle u|v\rangle^*.⟨v∣u⟩=⟨u∣v⟩∗.
(13)

Putting a ket before a bra gives an outer product instead:

∣u⟩⟨v∣=uv†.\boxed{|u\rangle\langle v|=\mathbf u\mathbf v^\dagger}.∣u⟩⟨v∣=uv†​.
(14)

This result is a matrix. In particular, ∣e⟩⟨e∣|e\rangle\langle e|∣e⟩⟨e∣ is the projector onto the direction of a normalized vector ∣e⟩|e\rangle∣e⟩.

Orthogonality and completeness¶

We already did this for real vectors: u⋅v=uTv\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=\mathbf u^T\mathbf vu⋅v=uTv, and orthogonal vectors satisfy uTv=0\mathbf u^T\mathbf v=0uTv=0. For complex vectors, the construction is the same except that we replace the transpose by the conjugate transpose.

Thus two complex vectors are orthogonal when ⟨u∣v⟩=u†v=0\langle u|v\rangle=\mathbf u^\dagger\mathbf v=0⟨u∣v⟩=u†v=0. An orthonormal set satisfies

⟨en∣em⟩=en†em=δnm.\langle e_n|e_m\rangle =\mathbf e_n^\dagger\mathbf e_m =\delta_{nm}.⟨en​∣em​⟩=en†​em​=δnm​.
(15)

For example, the complex vectors

e1=12(1i),e2=12(1−i)\mathbf e_1=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\i\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf e_2=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-i\end{pmatrix}e1​=2​1​(1i​),e2​=2​1​(1−i​)
(16)

both have norm one, and their inner product is (1+(−i)(−i))/2=0(1+(-i)(-i))/2=0(1+(−i)(−i))/2=0. They form an orthonormal basis of C2\mathbb C^2C2.

Expanding in an orthonormal basis¶

If e1,…,en\mathbf e_1,\ldots,\mathbf e_ne1​,…,en​ form an orthonormal basis, any vector can be expanded as

v=∑m=1ncmem,cm=⟨em∣v⟩=em†v.\mathbf v=\sum_{m=1}^n c_m\mathbf e_m,\qquad c_m=\langle e_m|v\rangle =\mathbf e_m^\dagger\mathbf v.v=m=1∑n​cm​em​,cm​=⟨em​∣v⟩=em†​v.
(17)

To find a coefficient, multiply the expansion by em†\mathbf e_m^\daggerem†​; orthogonality removes every other term.

Theorem 1 (Completeness of an orthonormal basis)

For a full orthonormal basis of Cn\mathbb C^nCn,

∑m=1n∣em⟩⟨em∣=∑m=1nemem†=I.\sum_{m=1}^n|e_m\rangle\langle e_m| =\sum_{m=1}^n\mathbf e_m\mathbf e_m^\dagger =\mathbf I.m=1∑n​∣em​⟩⟨em​∣=m=1∑n​em​em†​=I.
(18)
Proof 2

Applying the sum to any vector gives

(∑m∣em⟩⟨em∣)∣v⟩=∑m⟨em∣v⟩∣em⟩=∣v⟩.\left(\sum_m|e_m\rangle\langle e_m|\right)|v\rangle =\sum_m\langle e_m|v\rangle|e_m\rangle =|v\rangle.(m∑​∣em​⟩⟨em​∣)∣v⟩=m∑​⟨em​∣v⟩∣em​⟩=∣v⟩.
(19)

It therefore acts as the identity on every vector.

If we sum over only part of the basis, we obtain the projector onto that subspace, not the identity. Orthogonality also gives

∥v∥2=∑m∣cm∣2.\|\mathbf v\|^2=\sum_m|c_m|^2.∥v∥2=m∑​∣cm​∣2.
(20)

For the two basis vectors above, (1,0)T=(e1+e2)/2(1,0)^T=(\mathbf e_1+\mathbf e_2)/\sqrt2(1,0)T=(e1​+e2​)/2​: each coefficient has squared magnitude 1/21/21/2.

The construction of an orthonormal basis by subtracting projections is developed in Projections and Gram–Schmidt. For complex vectors, use the conjugate transpose in each projection.

Hermitian matrices¶

In the normal-modes lecture, our system of springs and masses gave us a real symmetric matrix. That symmetry was important: its eigenvalues were real, and eigenvectors belonging to different eigenvalues were orthogonal.

Now our vectors and matrices can be complex. What plays the same role as a real symmetric matrix in a complex vector space? Many physical systems, especially quantum observables and the generators of closed-system evolution, are described by Hermitian matrices. These matrices again have real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues.

A matrix is Hermitian when

H†=H.\mathbf H^\dagger=\mathbf H.H†=H.
(21)

For a real matrix, the dagger is just the transpose, so the Hermitian condition reduces to the symmetric condition. A Hermitian matrix has real diagonal entries, and entries across the diagonal are complex conjugates:

H=(abb∗d),a,d∈R.\mathbf H=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b^*&d\end{pmatrix}, \qquad a,d\in\mathbb R.H=(ab∗​bd​),a,d∈R.
(22)

This definition gives us the complex version of the structure we used in normal modes. The next theorem makes its two key consequences precise.

Theorem 2 (Eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a Hermitian matrix)

A Hermitian matrix has real eigenvalues. Eigenvectors belonging to distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal.

Proof 3 (Bra-ket notation)

Assume H\mathbf HH is Hermitian, so H†=H\mathbf H^\dagger=\mathbf HH†=H. Let ∣un⟩|u_n\rangle∣un​⟩ and ∣um⟩|u_m\rangle∣um​⟩ be nonzero eigenvectors:

H∣un⟩=λn∣un⟩,H∣um⟩=λm∣um⟩.\mathbf H|u_n\rangle=\lambda_n|u_n\rangle, \qquad \mathbf H|u_m\rangle=\lambda_m|u_m\rangle.H∣un​⟩=λn​∣un​⟩,H∣um​⟩=λm​∣um​⟩.
(23)

We have not yet assumed that the eigenvalues are real or distinct. Start with the scalar matrix element

⟨un∣H∣um⟩.\langle u_n|\mathbf H|u_m\rangle.⟨un​∣H∣um​⟩.
(24)

First let H\mathbf HH act on the ket to its right:

⟨un∣H∣um⟩=λm⟨un∣um⟩.\langle u_n|\mathbf H|u_m\rangle =\lambda_m\langle u_n|u_m\rangle.⟨un​∣H∣um​⟩=λm​⟨un​∣um​⟩.
(25)

We can also let H\mathbf HH act to the left. Taking the dagger of the first eigenvalue equation gives

(H∣un⟩)†=(λn∣un⟩)†,(\mathbf H|u_n\rangle)^\dagger =(\lambda_n|u_n\rangle)^\dagger,(H∣un​⟩)†=(λn​∣un​⟩)†,
(26)

and therefore

⟨un∣H†=λn∗⟨un∣.\langle u_n|\mathbf H^\dagger =\lambda_n^*\langle u_n|.⟨un​∣H†=λn∗​⟨un​∣.
(27)

Because H†=H\mathbf H^\dagger=\mathbf HH†=H,

⟨un∣H∣um⟩=λn∗⟨un∣um⟩.\langle u_n|\mathbf H|u_m\rangle =\lambda_n^*\langle u_n|u_m\rangle.⟨un​∣H∣um​⟩=λn∗​⟨un​∣um​⟩.
(28)

We have evaluated the same scalar in two ways, so

(λm−λn∗)⟨un∣um⟩=0.(\lambda_m-\lambda_n^*)\langle u_n|u_m\rangle=0.(λm​−λn∗​)⟨un​∣um​⟩=0.
(29)

There are two conclusions. First, set m=nm=nm=n:

(λn−λn∗)⟨un∣un⟩=0.(\lambda_n-\lambda_n^*)\langle u_n|u_n\rangle=0.(λn​−λn∗​)⟨un​∣un​⟩=0.
(30)

Because ∣un⟩|u_n\rangle∣un​⟩ is nonzero, ⟨un∣un⟩>0\langle u_n|u_n\rangle>0⟨un​∣un​⟩>0. Therefore λn=λn∗\lambda_n=\lambda_n^*λn​=λn∗​, so every eigenvalue is real.

Second, choose two distinct eigenvalues, λn≠λm\lambda_n\ne\lambda_mλn​=λm​. Since the eigenvalues are real,

(λm−λn)⟨un∣um⟩=0.(\lambda_m-\lambda_n)\langle u_n|u_m\rangle=0.(λm​−λn​)⟨un​∣um​⟩=0.
(31)

The first factor is nonzero, so ⟨un∣um⟩=0\langle u_n|u_m\rangle=0⟨un​∣um​⟩=0. Thus eigenvectors belonging to distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal.

Although we proved this using complex vectors, the real symmetric case is included: for a real matrix, the conjugate transpose is just the transpose.

A standard complex example: the Pauli matrices¶

Three Hermitian matrices that appear throughout quantum mechanics are the Pauli matrices:

σx=(0110),σy=(0−ii0),σz=(100−1).\boldsymbol\sigma_x= \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \boldsymbol\sigma_y= \begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \boldsymbol\sigma_z= \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.σx​=(01​10​),σy​=(0i​−i0​),σz​=(10​0−1​).
(32)

The matrices σx\boldsymbol\sigma_xσx​ and σz\boldsymbol\sigma_zσz​ are real and symmetric. The matrix σy\boldsymbol\sigma_yσy​ is genuinely complex, but its off-diagonal entries are complex conjugates, so σy†=σy\boldsymbol\sigma_y^\dagger=\boldsymbol\sigma_yσy†​=σy​. All three are therefore Hermitian.

Each matrix has eigenvalues +1 and -1. One normalized choice of eigenvectors is

λ=+1λ=−1σx12(11)12(1−1)σy12(1i)12(1−i)σz(10)(01)\begin{array}{c|cc} &\lambda=+1&\lambda=-1\\ \hline \boldsymbol\sigma_x &\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix} &\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}\\[1.2em] \boldsymbol\sigma_y &\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\i\end{pmatrix} &\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-i\end{pmatrix}\\[1.2em] \boldsymbol\sigma_z &\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix} &\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix} \end{array}σx​σy​σz​​λ=+12​1​(11​)2​1​(1i​)(10​)​λ=−12​1​(1−1​)2​1​(1−i​)(01​)​​
(33)

You can check each pair by multiplying the matrix into the proposed vector. For the genuinely complex example,

σy12(1i)=12(1i),σy12(1−i)=−12(1−i).\boldsymbol\sigma_y\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\i\end{pmatrix} =\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\i\end{pmatrix},\qquad \boldsymbol\sigma_y\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-i\end{pmatrix} =-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-i\end{pmatrix}.σy​2​1​(1i​)=2​1​(1i​),σy​2​1​(1−i​)=−2​1​(1−i​).
(34)

The two eigenvectors for each matrix are orthogonal. Thus these familiar matrices show both conclusions of the theorem: Hermitian matrices have real eigenvalues, and eigenvectors with different eigenvalues are orthogonal.

Theorem 3 (Hermitian quadratic forms are real)

If H\mathbf HH is Hermitian, then

q=v†Hvq=\mathbf v^\dagger\mathbf H\mathbf vq=v†Hv
(35)

is real for every complex vector v\mathbf vv.

Proof 4

The quantity qqq is a scalar. Take its complex conjugate. Because the conjugate transpose of a scalar is the same as its complex conjugate,

q∗=(v†Hv)†=v†H†v=v†Hv=q.q^*=(\mathbf v^\dagger\mathbf H\mathbf v)^\dagger =\mathbf v^\dagger\mathbf H^\dagger\mathbf v =\mathbf v^\dagger\mathbf H\mathbf v=q.q∗=(v†Hv)†=v†H†v=v†Hv=q.
(36)

Thus q∗=qq^*=qq∗=q, so qqq is real.

Connection to quantum mechanics¶

In quantum mechanics, an observable is a physical quantity that we can measure, such as position, momentum, or energy. The result of a measurement must be a real number. For a normalized state ψ\boldsymbol\psiψ, the expectation value ψ†Hψ\boldsymbol\psi^\dagger\mathbf H\boldsymbol\psiψ†Hψ must also be real. The theorem we just proved shows why Hermitian matrices have exactly the structure we need. This leads to a special correspondence between observables and Hermitian matrices, or more generally, Hermitian operators:

quantum observable⟷Hermitian operator H.\boxed{\text{quantum observable}} \quad\longleftrightarrow\quad \boxed{\text{Hermitian operator }\mathbf H}.quantum observable​⟷Hermitian operator H​.
(37)

Suppose

Hun=λnun.\mathbf H\mathbf u_n=\lambda_n\mathbf u_n.Hun​=λn​un​.
(38)

The real eigenvalue λn\lambda_nλn​ is a possible result of measuring the observable. The normalized eigenvector un\mathbf u_nun​ represents a state in which that result is definite:

possible measurement result λn⟷real eigenvalue of H,\boxed{\text{possible measurement result }\lambda_n} \quad\longleftrightarrow\quad \boxed{\text{real eigenvalue of }\mathbf H},possible measurement result λn​​⟷real eigenvalue of H​,
(39)
state with definite result λn⟷normalized eigenvector un.\boxed{\text{state with definite result }\lambda_n} \quad\longleftrightarrow\quad \boxed{\text{normalized eigenvector }\mathbf u_n}.state with definite result λn​​⟷normalized eigenvector un​​.
(40)

Because a Hermitian matrix has orthogonal eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues, states with different definite measurement results are orthogonal. A general quantum state does not have to be one eigenvector: it can be a superposition

ψ=∑ncnun,cn=un†ψ.\boldsymbol\psi=\sum_n c_n\mathbf u_n, \qquad c_n=\mathbf u_n^\dagger\boldsymbol\psi.ψ=n∑​cn​un​,cn​=un†​ψ.
(41)

If the eigenvectors form an orthonormal basis and ψ\boldsymbol\psiψ is normalized, then ∣cn∣2|c_n|^2∣cn​∣2 is the probability of obtaining the result λn\lambda_nλn​. Thus the eigenvectors identify the definite-outcome states, while their real eigenvalues give the possible measured values.

Unitary matrices¶

In Orthogonal Transformations and Rotations, we asked which real matrices preserve the length of every real vector. If b=Ma\mathbf b=\mathbf M\mathbf ab=Ma, requiring ∥b∥2=∥a∥2\|\mathbf b\|^2=\|\mathbf a\|^2∥b∥2=∥a∥2 for every a\mathbf aa led to

MTM=I.\mathbf M^T\mathbf M=\mathbf I.MTM=I.
(42)

We can now ask the same question for a complex vector. Let a matrix U\mathbf UU transform v\mathbf vv into v′\mathbf v'v′:

v′=Uv.\mathbf v'=\mathbf U\mathbf v.v′=Uv.
(43)

Using the complex squared length ∥v∥2=v†v\|\mathbf v\|^2=\mathbf v^\dagger\mathbf v∥v∥2=v†v, the transformed vector has

∥v′∥2=v′†v′=(Uv)†(Uv)=v†U†Uv.\begin{aligned} \|\mathbf v'\|^2 &=\mathbf v'^\dagger\mathbf v'\\ &=(\mathbf U\mathbf v)^\dagger(\mathbf U\mathbf v)\\ &=\mathbf v^\dagger\mathbf U^\dagger\mathbf U\mathbf v. \end{aligned}∥v′∥2​=v′†v′=(Uv)†(Uv)=v†U†Uv.​
(44)

For this to equal v†v\mathbf v^\dagger\mathbf vv†v for every complex vector v\mathbf vv, we require

U†U=I.\mathbf U^\dagger\mathbf U=\mathbf I.U†U=I.
(45)

This is the complex version of the orthogonal-matrix condition: the transpose is replaced by the conjugate transpose.

Definition 1 (Unitary matrix)

A square complex matrix U\mathbf UU is unitary when

U†U=UU†=I,U−1=U†.\mathbf U^\dagger\mathbf U=\mathbf U\mathbf U^\dagger=\mathbf I, \qquad \mathbf U^{-1}=\mathbf U^\dagger.U†U=UU†=I,U−1=U†.
(46)

For a square matrix, U†U=I\mathbf U^\dagger\mathbf U=\mathbf IU†U=I makes U†\mathbf U^\daggerU† the inverse of U\mathbf UU, so it also gives UU†=I\mathbf U\mathbf U^\dagger=\mathbf IUU†=I.

Theorem 4 (Unitary transformations preserve inner products)

For a unitary U\mathbf UU,

(Uu)†(Uv)=u†v.(\mathbf U\mathbf u)^\dagger(\mathbf U\mathbf v) =\mathbf u^\dagger\mathbf v.(Uu)†(Uv)=u†v.
(47)

In particular, lengths and orthogonality are preserved.

Proof 5

Using the conjugate-transpose product rule,

(Uu)†(Uv)=u†U†Uv=u†v.(\mathbf U\mathbf u)^\dagger(\mathbf U\mathbf v) =\mathbf u^\dagger\mathbf U^\dagger\mathbf U\mathbf v =\mathbf u^\dagger\mathbf v.(Uu)†(Uv)=u†U†Uv=u†v.
(48)

Set u=v\mathbf u=\mathbf vu=v to obtain preservation of squared length.

Example 1 (A unitary transformation that mixes components)

Consider

U=12(1ii1).\mathbf U=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&i\\i&1\end{pmatrix}.U=2​1​(1i​i1​).
(49)

Taking the conjugate transpose and multiplying gives

U†U=12(1−i−i1)(1ii1)=I,\mathbf U^\dagger\mathbf U =\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&-i\\-i&1\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}1&i\\i&1\end{pmatrix} =\mathbf I,U†U=21​(1−i​−i1​)(1i​i1​)=I,
(50)

so U\mathbf UU is unitary. Now apply it to the first coordinate vector:

v=(10),v′=Uv=12(1i).\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathbf v'=\mathbf U\mathbf v =\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\i\end{pmatrix}.v=(10​),v′=Uv=2​1​(1i​).
(51)

The individual components changed, but the squared length did not:

∥v∥2=1,∥v′∥2=∣12∣2+∣i2∣2=1.\|\mathbf v\|^2=1, \qquad \|\mathbf v'\|^2 =\left|\frac1{\sqrt2}\right|^2 +\left|\frac{i}{\sqrt2}\right|^2=1.∥v∥2=1,∥v′∥2=∣∣​2​1​∣∣​2+∣∣​2​i​∣∣​2=1.
(52)

This is a complex rotation: in fact, U=eiπσx/4\mathbf U=e^{i\pi\boldsymbol\sigma_x/4}U=eiπσx​/4. In quantum mechanics, this transformation can be pictured as a rotation of a state on the Bloch sphere. We will return to that picture later.

Connection to quantum mechanics: transformations¶

In quantum mechanics, we describe a state by a complex vector. A reversible transformation of a closed quantum system must preserve the total probability, and it is represented by a unitary matrix:

unitary matrix U⟷reversible transformation of a quantum state.\boxed{\text{unitary matrix }\mathbf U} \quad\longleftrightarrow\quad \boxed{\text{reversible transformation of a quantum state}}.unitary matrix U​⟷reversible transformation of a quantum state​.
(53)

If the initial state is ψ\boldsymbol\psiψ, the transformed state is

ψ′=Uψ.\boldsymbol\psi'=\mathbf U\boldsymbol\psi.ψ′=Uψ.
(54)

The squared length of a normalized state is its total probability. Unitarity guarantees

∥ψ′∥2=ψ†U†Uψ=ψ†ψ=1.\|\boldsymbol\psi'\|^2 =\boldsymbol\psi^\dagger\mathbf U^\dagger\mathbf U\boldsymbol\psi =\boldsymbol\psi^\dagger\boldsymbol\psi=1.∥ψ′∥2=ψ†U†Uψ=ψ†ψ=1.
(55)

Time evolution is one of the most important examples. A unitary matrix takes the state at time t0t_0t0​ to the state at time ttt:

ψ(t)=U(t,t0)ψ(t0).\boldsymbol\psi(t)=\mathbf U(t,t_0)\boldsymbol\psi(t_0).ψ(t)=U(t,t0​)ψ(t0​).
(56)

Unitary evolution is reversible: applying U†\mathbf U^\daggerU† undoes U\mathbf UU. If ψ′=Uψ\boldsymbol\psi'=\mathbf U\boldsymbol\psiψ′=Uψ, then

U†ψ′=U†Uψ=ψ.\mathbf U^\dagger\boldsymbol\psi' =\mathbf U^\dagger\mathbf U\boldsymbol\psi =\boldsymbol\psi.U†ψ′=U†Uψ=ψ.
(57)

For real matrices, the unitary condition reduces to the orthogonal condition. Do not confuse this with the Hermitian condition: Hermitian means H†=H\mathbf H^\dagger=\mathbf HH†=H; unitary means U†=U−1\mathbf U^\dagger=\mathbf U^{-1}U†=U−1.

The example above shows what this allows: the state can change from one component to a superposition with probabilities (1/2,1/2)(1/2,1/2)(1/2,1/2) while the total probability remains one.

Eigenvalues of a unitary matrix¶

Theorem 5 (Unitary eigenvalues have unit magnitude)

If Uv=λv\mathbf U\mathbf v=\lambda\mathbf vUv=λv with v≠0\mathbf v\ne0v=0, then ∣λ∣=1|\lambda|=1∣λ∣=1.

Proof 6

Since a unitary matrix preserves length,

∥v∥2=∥Uv∥2=∥λv∥2=∣λ∣2∥v∥2.\|\mathbf v\|^2=\|\mathbf U\mathbf v\|^2 =\|\lambda\mathbf v\|^2=|\lambda|^2\|\mathbf v\|^2.∥v∥2=∥Uv∥2=∥λv∥2=∣λ∣2∥v∥2.
(58)

Because v≠0\mathbf v\ne0v=0, its squared norm is positive. Dividing by ∥v∥2\|\mathbf v\|^2∥v∥2 gives ∣λ∣2=1|\lambda|^2=1∣λ∣2=1, and therefore ∣λ∣=1|\lambda|=1∣λ∣=1.

Thus a unitary eigenvalue can be written as eiθe^{i\theta}eiθ: along an eigenvector, the transformation changes phase but not magnitude. This completes the complex version of our earlier argument for orthogonal matrices.
